utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If we can just make slightly longer breaks, please. You were asked and you answered about the influence, that is to say, the autonomy of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, so I will ask you to have a look at one document which you sent. It's 1D9862.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's nothing on the screen here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at this. It's 1992. I can't see the exact date but it's somewhere here. The 10th of July it seems.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The 10th of August, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or perhaps it's earlier. I can't see it but we'll see. Perhaps the 1st of August. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at what your proposal was with regard to these people and can you please tell the Chamber how much of this proposal was adopted. You proposed --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please scroll down or turn into the following page in the Serbian version. And in English also, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You proposed Nedeljko Lajic, Colonel Subotic, and Petar Markovic. Were all three of them in the government?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat, please. Petar Markovic, yes. Subotic, yes. And who else did you say, Lajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, the minister of transportation.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they were in the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And up on the page we can see that you proposed Bijelic Slobodan, Jovo Todorovic, Vukasin Basic, Nenad Balaban, and up there Radoslav Brdjanin for construction works. Somebody else as well, Nikola Herceg for the government. Were all these people in the government and were these wishes of the Autonomous Region of Krajina taken into account?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that our agreement on the founding of the Republika Srpska and constituting of the Assembly was that regions would be equally represented in the top organs, that is to say, the government and the ministries of Republika Srpska, and that was honoured. We had no objections. All the people we proposed were appointed to the relevant ministries and relevant posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D4026, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In cross-examination it was suggested to you that the goal of regionalisation was to break up Bosnia and Herzegovina. Can you tell us, first of all, until when did Bosnia-Herzegovina de facto and de jure continue to be an integral part of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think until April or May it was a part of Yugoslavia. Perhaps it was May, the 5th of May, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mean when did it stop being in Yugoslavia when it was admitted to the UN?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could put it that way. I think it was admitted on the 6th of April, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of May it was acknowledged and in late May it was admitted to the UN.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I did not understand your question. Up until was Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: De facto and de jure a part of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, until it became independent and until it was recognised by the UN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's bear in mind this is not a dialogue between Mr. Karadzic and the witness, where the witness can put questions to Mr. Karadzic, who can then answer them and they can continue. So Dr. Karadzic needs to refrain from providing the witness with helpful information that advances the answers he's looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But the dates themselves are undisputed. This is why I wanted to touch on this. Mr. Kupresanin, when did the talks and activities about regionalisation begin in 1991? That is to say, when that happened, was Bosnia then still an integral part of Yugoslavia and its constitutional and legal system?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In such a Yugoslavia, were the Muslims, the Croats, and the Serbs all in one state?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the Muslims and the Croats want to continue living together with the Serbs in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the Muslim and Croat political parties which were pushing Bosnia towards secession, did they violate the constitution of the SFRY and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And as for the ARK, the Autonomous Region of Krajina, was it formed as an exclusively Serbian region and was that the first attempt at regionalisation or have there been other attempts before Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very title of the Autonomous Region of Krajina does not include the adjective Serbian, such as the Serbian autonomous districts in some other areas. We intentionally avoided this title and this adjective so that everyone would feel more comfortable and better and more at ease, as if they were at their own home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your interview from 2001, which is 65 ter 25608 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 25608, English page 8, Serbian page 12. It's line 43 here and Serbian pages number 12, English page 8 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, what number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Line 43 in English. Let me just check where it is here. "That idea of the region is to regionalise Bosnia" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure where we're headed, but here's what it appears to me. The -- our use of this interview in cross-examination does not give the accused carte blanche to lay out portions of the interview in a leading way to this witness that don't bear on those portions that were used in the cross-examination. So I don't think this was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the passage seems to be related to regionalisation --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- about which he put already some questions. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But this is not a document. This is what the witness said before, Mr. President, and this is just an attempt to lead the witness to something he said -- he can elicit information from this witness. If he needs a document, for example, to refresh a specific recollection of the witness, that would be fair, but all it is now is trawling through portions of this thing in a leading manner to get the witness to affirm. That's fine in cross-examination, as you know, but that's not a proper method of direct or re-direct and we've already crossed that bridge on many occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't agree with Mr. Tieger. The Prosecution used this interview selectively to try to show that statements that were made at that time were inconsistent with his position today, and I think Dr. Karadzic is now fully entitled to put portions of those interviews so the witness can explain his position on those same issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I -- it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will just --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just wait. I'm waiting for the interpretation. When you stand, I will give you the floor. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And sorry for jumping the gun. I acknowledged that essentially when I spoke earlier, and that is where there are portions that are -- may be properly contextualised, that is, portions of the interview that were raised before that can require a proper contextualisation or the accused considers need to be contextualised by other parts of the interview related to that specific portion that was raised, that's appropriate and I said that. But that doesn't mean that the accused can go to any part of the interview with respect to any issue that was raised in cross-examination, and that's, I think, what Mr. Robinson may have inadvertently suggested; that would not be appropriate, that would be leading. So with that caveat, my objection stands, and I think that's what's happening in this particular instance. I don't believe that there's anything about what I see on this page that implicates a portion of the interview that I raised in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. -- could we collapse the document for the moment. Mr. Kupresanin, could you kindly take off your headphones for the moment. Mr. Karadzic put some questions about regionalisation, for example, whether at that time the -- Bosnia was still part of Yugoslavia and he dealt with some constitutional issues. And here it says the regionalisation was already an old idea at the time. Why do you think this is leading, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, because, Mr. President, the -- it's leading because he's saying: Let me tell you what you said before, that's what you said or that's right, isn't it? So the only reason this would be relevant is if it -- if the specific issue was raised in a manner to suggest that the witness had never taken that position before or if another portion of the interview had been cited where the witness contradicted this point and now they want to show: Well, in another portion of the interview he said something more consistent with the information in his statement. But simply to use this document, to put it in front of the witness, to say: Now I'm asking you some questions about a general topic that wasn't raised in cross-examination, which is where we are right now, Mr. Karadzic is focusing on information that was already in the statement and he's returning back to the statement to try to make an advocacy point. And he now uses the interview to take the witness to things he wants the witness to say. And if the witness -- he can just ask the witness the question here. If the witness affirms that proposition, he has the information; if the witness doesn't affirm that proposition, then the Court knows what the witness remembers today. And then if the accused wants to take him back to refresh his recollection, he can, but then you have a much better idea of what this witness knows now rather than what Dr. Karadzic wants him to simply affirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think this is really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, when the Prosecution used this interview during the course of its cross-examination to show that the witness was giving answers different than what he said before and was therefore not credible, that opened the door for Dr. Karadzic to use any portion of that interview to show that he was consistent -- what he says now is consistent with what he said then on any topic covered by the cross-examination, not whether -- it's not restricted to any portions -- and he can do that by putting what the witness -- showing the witness what he said before and asking him how that relates to what actually is the fact and the witness can give his testimony as to what he believes the case. So this is a very hyper-technical approach that Mr. Tieger is taking and we don't act in that spirit during his cross-examination because he asked a lot of questions that could have been objected to which were convoluted and complex and we let it go for the purpose of -- just a free flow of information and exchange. But in this instance, I think Mr. Tieger is being hyper-technical and unduly restricting the examination -- the re-direct examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: If I may add --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- Tieger first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Last point from me then. I take very seriously Mr. Robinson's suggestion that I somehow may be running afoul of the spirit of the courtroom which has developed because I appreciate the -- what I think has been an exemplary attitude in the courtroom on the side of everyone in the courtroom, and I don't want to do anything to impede that. Let me just say that it's not the cross -- it's not the Prosecution's point that this witness was incapable ever of saying anything consistent with what he said before; that wasn't the nature of the impeachment. So he's not really rehabilitated if he finds some points he's consistent on. The point was he was being inconsistent on particular points of particular interest. So to go back and identify all the points on which he was consistent doesn't really advance the ball in that way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Tieger. Let's consider in this way, one option the Chamber could have taken when you tendered the part of the interview was to admit it in its entirety --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, this may help. I don't mean to interrupt. I'm withdrawing the objection in light of Mr. Robinson's comments. That's what I was going to say. I just didn't want to be misunderstood what the impeachment was about. Sorry to interrupt, but I thought that might help the Court. I accept that we are in a position where we're trying to be as accommodating as possible and not have unnecessary obstacles. I think this is helpful in the sense that the cross-examination -- the nature of the cross-examination is not misunderstood and the nature of the attempt at rehabilitation is not misunderstood, but let me not be in the way any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Gospodine Kupresanin, you may use your headphones now. Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, we'll add that page to the P6510, I don't remember the number -- yes, P6510. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I asked all this because of page 22 of yesterday's transcript and the minutes of our meeting dated the 14th of February --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin, on the 14th of February, 1992, were we all still in Yugoslavia and was Bosnia in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You confirmed again that you wanted the Muslims and the Croats -- or did you want the Muslims and the Croats to feel comfortable within the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. We wanted to expand the region so as to include the Jajce municipality, the Cazin Krajina, and a number of municipalities where the Muslims were the dominant population, mostly Muslims. The goal was to begin functioning economically in the first place. Kladusa, where Fikret Abdic was the main man, where he had one of the most powerful processing industries in the former Yugoslavia, I asked him several times by fax to begin co-operating with the area where I lived, which is called Lijevce Polje. It's a huge valley where food is produced in large quantities, meat, grain, and mostly vegetables, that we should serve as the material basis and they would develop further their processing industry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see page 9 of this document in English and page 13 in Serbian. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From here 37, it's line 10 here in Serbian, where you say: "Well, the tendency was to create regions in Bosnia-Herzegovina ... from the beginning of 1991 ..." And then you say later: "... the Serbian Autonomous Regions, in order to avoid the Serbian prefix, we used Autonomous Region because there were Muslims and Croats who lived here, and all of us together, in order not to irritate them, eventually we called it the Autonomous Region." Does that correspond to the state of minds as it existed at the time?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was supposed to correspond and I believe that at first it did. Last time when answering a Prosecutor's question I said that I have my personal view of who we are in this area. I believe that 100 per cent we are one and the same people and that everything that went on later is pure horror. I don't think it was the will and the decision of the people. International intelligence services drew us into something that's called war. I believe that people on all sides had the goodwill to live in peace because we are normal peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This position of yours not to irritate the Muslims and the Croats, did it result in their participation in the work?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show the following page as well in English and in Serbian too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This, Mr. Kupresanin, where you say that the question was of the 168 deputies in the Assembly, were there any Croats and Muslims? And you say that the percentage reflected -- [In English] A percentage of different ethnicities in different municipalities that number was represented [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. And a bit lower down the question is: [In English] "So I come back to the question: How many Muslims were in the ARK Assembly?" And your response was: "Well, I don't know exactly. At the beginning" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second. Just a second. Probably we need the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Sorry. From the line 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And your response was from 31 and then 46. [Interpretation] Does this correspond to the situation which existed at the time and why, in your view, did the Muslim and Croatian participation in the Krajina Assembly begin to dwindle?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The presence of the Muslims and the Croatians in the Assembly was adequate to their participation at the municipal level. Why did they become less and less active? Because the parties that were in power and the political turmoil in all Bosnia-Herzegovina, but primarily in Sarajevo, primarily influenced them so that they began to withdraw from the political life in the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Whatever was going on in Sarajevo was reflected in a way in the outlying areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please add these two pages?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Another question with regard to this subject matter. You were asked about what happened in Kotor Varos. What was your role and what was my role in these events, to the best of your knowledge then?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I informed you and you told me: Mr. Kupresanin, I trust you, you will do that best. Actually, I told you what was going on in Kotor Varos, there were killings going on all the time, more and more from one day to the other. Also an incredible crime was committed; that is to say, people were impaled and then roasted like pigs. Then also, they used saws to saw off people's limbs. I did not investigate. I thought that we who figured prominently in those areas should be involved in resolving the problems in that area. I, Mr. Komarica, two other priests, a hodza, Nikola Gabelic, the president of the HDZ -- the president of the HDZ did not want to take part. His policy was: The worse the better. I asked him so many times to come along with me, to do something about it. However, Emir Busatlic, a doctor, a dentist, he appeared fortunately and we as a team tried to find a peaceful solution. If necessary, I can go on talking about this; if not, I will stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was my position with regard to care for civilians and the fate of civilians in Kotor Varos, do you remember? Did you have insight?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As usual, you said that maximum care should be taken of civilians. When I say "civilians," I am not speaking about adults to a very high degree; I'm talking about women, children, and old people. And that was being done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about dismissals of directors, managers. Was it directors of private companies or equity companies that were being replaced?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just public enterprises, state-owned enterprises.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which political party is accountable for the successful performance of state-owned enterprises in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly the party that won the elections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Kupresanin, if you clarify this. A minute ago you talked about civilians. You said, I quote: "I'm talking about women, children, and old people. And that was being done." And before that you said you are not talking about adults to a very high degree. Could you clarify what you meant by that? You're not speaking about adults to a very high degree.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The accent were the women and children, that's what was accentuated, because physically they are under threat, they are sensitive being outdoors when there is a terrible storm outside, and there was a storm at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then how about the male civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was with the men, the civilians. Of course we talked about the different subjects. While I was there talking to them, there were some European media that were present. Everything was filmed. They brought me weapons. There weren't even our soldiers there. There were two or three soldiers who took these weapons and put them into trucks, and then they went into buses. Then I noticed that people were asking civilians for money and then I protested, and then I said: What's going to happen if they don't have any money? And then they weren't being asked for money anymore because many of them did not have any money in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 50 marks, that's what they were asked to give.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I will leave it at that. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For what purpose were those 50 marks asked for?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The explanation was for the bus, for that service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Brisevo was mentioned. Was Brisevo an undefended village with civilians that some armed formation of the Serbs attacked? Was there any combat there or was this an unarmed village?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was unarmed. There was no combat there. I don't know which military formations attacked the village. I could not receive any more detailed information. These women that I saw did not want to discuss any subject. They just said: We want to leave. There is no going back for us. We don't want to be reminded, and so on and so forth. I said yesterday that these figures constantly varied, 80, 60, the numbers of persons killed. So I really don't know how many victims there were there. I could not enter Brisevo. The army brought us there and that's where we stayed, and then Catholic mass was celebrated in a church and that's it. At any rate, we promised that that would happen and that did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also asked about a telegram that was shown to you -- or actually, a telegram was shown to you -- actually, let me ask you this first: Was military rule imposed in any municipality in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There was no military rule?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of that from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were shown an intercept from the 23rd of July, 1991, as a reaction to your assertion that you did not talk to me about the establishment of the Krajina. On the 30th of July, 1991, was this intercept about the establishment of the Krajina or was it about a referendum that somebody had proposed and that I had refused --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's call up the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe the Court can see readily what a leading question this was. And we can call up the document, but now the witness has been informed about what the accused's position is and what kind of answer he wants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you follow, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency, but I think that the entire telegram was not shown to the witness. He was only asked about a single sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you do not follow. Read your question again and the way it was formatted, it's very much leading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand now, but could the telegram be shown now, or rather, that intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit number? Or 65 ter?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm looking for it. All right. It's hard to find and I don't want to waste any time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it D1084?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Possibly. If it's the 23rd of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think it's P1084.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's referred to in paragraph 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's one of the associated exhibits, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, P1084.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do cast a glance at the first page and then let's take a look at this second page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Next page in Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this. The fourth part where you are speaking, that they reached some kind of agreement concerning a referendum. I heard about that today, and then four paragraphs down I'm speaking about that referendum, saying that things should not be done, anything that would violate the constitution. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, but that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Kupresanin. I have no further questions. Thank you for having made this effort to come here and testify, and thank you for having taken care of all the citizens of the Krajina as I had hoped.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV KUPRESANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you to the Judges, the Prosecutors, and Defence counsel. I enjoyed this. This was pleasant. I didn't have any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, unless my colleagues have a question for you, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. You're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ah, thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And your next witness is Poplasen?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Even if we can conclude this witness's evidence today, I don't think we can hear part of Mr. Krajisnik's cross-examination today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Poplasen. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Good morning to you, Mr. Poplasen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, honourable Judges. Good morning to all the participants in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Poplasen, I must draw your attention to a certain rule that we have here at the international Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Good morning to you once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for having already felt that pauses should be made between questions and answers because we are speaking the same language. Did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Yes, I gave a statement in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D9193 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that statement before you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is the statement that I provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read and sign the statement?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Yes, I read it in its entirety and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the last page so that he could identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Yes, entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today in this courtroom live, would your answers basically be the same?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Basically they would be the same, but I did not learn this text by heart so it's not that I can remember all of it that way. Basically they would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this statement according to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that you're tendering some associated exhibits as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: There are six associated exhibits that we're tendering, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Were they on the 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll assign -- we'll admit them and assign the numbers. Shall we do that now?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 92 ter statement will be Exhibit D4027, 65 ter number 1566 will be Exhibit D4028 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They will be given numbers from D4028 to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the order of their numbers. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to read out the summary of Professor Nikola Poplasen's statement in English. [In English] Nikola Poplasen was appointed a member of the Political Council of the SDS in late 1990. In April 1992 he became adviser to the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of BH, and in June 1992 he was appointed commissioner of the Republika Srpska Presidency for Vogosca municipality. The situation in Sarajevo and Vogosca was chaotic. The SDA acted without heed to the wishes of the Serbs and appointed company directors and municipal leaders. The majority of the directors were Muslims. The barricades in Vogosca started springing up throughout the town at about the same time. The breakdown in security, lack of trust, and fear forced all sides to erect barricades and establish check-points in areas where they were the majority. Initially people thought that the problems would be resolved by agreement, but when the barricades and clashes started, most people began to relocate of their own accord to areas where they were in majority and where they thought they would be safer. Population relocation took place on all sides throughout the war, but this was merely and solely a result of the security problems arising from the chaos. The Crisis Staffs existed in Serbian municipalities. They were created because of the serious situation in the municipalities and throughout Republika Srpska. The Crisis Staff united the most important departments, politics, the army, and the police. Similarly, the War Presidencies were a form of organising government in the emerging situation and they had no specific role, particularly not in regard to planning the persecution of non-Serbs. At some point in June 1992, the Crisis Staff was disbanded in Vogosca and other Serbian municipalities. The War Commission was formed and civilian organs of government were established. The commission was formed in response to exceptionally difficult communication. Radio communication was difficult to establish. Between the first armed clashes in mid-1993 -- clashes 1992 until 1993, Vogosca had no telephone communications or electricity. The commission was a point of contact between the Republika Srpska Presidency and the government of the local authorities. Parts of Vogosca were constantly under fire from Muslim snipers. Several people were killed and wounded. The surrounding Muslim positions were dominant and overlooked most of Vogosca. Muslim forces largely benefitted from this advantage. No one in the Serbian side conducted a systematic campaign of shelling or sniping intended to inflict indiscriminate suffering of the civilian population. It would have been difficult for the Serbian forces in its territory to do this because of the position. As soon as Mr. Nikola Poplasen discovered the existence of places of detention, he wrote a letter to the minister of justice for these facilities to be inspected and integrated into the Republika Srpska judicial system. The RS leadership agreed that these issues should be dealt with in the manner prescribed by law and that this could not be a question dealt with by anyone in their own way. The Serbian leadership advocated that war was conducted while adhering to the international standards regulating this area, including the Geneva Protocols. There were volunteers operating in Vogosca. The procedure for receiving volunteers is regulated by law. They were all under the command of the VRS. The Serbian leadership and President Karadzic argued for all Serbian forces to be placed under a single command. Individual incidents did occur, but this was not the result of systematic or organised activity, nor was it with approval or knowledge of Serbian authorities. There was a law on abandoned property in Republika Srpska and the Serbian municipality authorities worked in accordance with it. This law was in force and was applied throughout the war. The intention was for the property to be preserved. There was a desire to prevent it being at the disposal of individuals and groups, and thus endeavours were made to regulate this issue by law. All the practical actions that were implemented, whether with deprivation or limitation of rights, related to and were equally applied to everyone, regardless of their ethnic or other affiliation. Dr. Karadzic advocated the fight for truth and justice and for the rights of other -- that others had. In mid-1992, Mr. Nikola Poplasen insisted on full reunification with the RSK. Since actual unification did not take place, he spoke with Dr. Karadzic, who explained that not one great power stood behind the Serbs and that Nikola Poplasen's radicalism was misguided, which further deepened the differences in their views. Dr. Karadzic's democratic approach and patience, even when an interlocutor's arguments were weak and unconvincing, led Nikola Poplasen to conclude that he was a non-authoritative -- that he was not a leader that could entrench his authority at the required level. Nikola Poplasen was an adviser in the Presidency of Republika Srpska, and no one ever conceived, organised or issued tasks for anyone to be persecuted based on their ethnicity. And that is a short summary. At that moment I do not have questions for President Poplasen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, in his statement Mr. Poplasen stated that he was appointed as commissioner of the Republika Srpska Presidency for Vogosca municipality. If you could clarify with the witness whether it's related to the War Commission he referred to and where he worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, shall I repeat this question or you were paying attention?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: I understood the question. It was addressed to you but I can answer to be of assistance. The commission was formed as a link between the War Presidency of Republika Srpska and they government of Republika Srpska, and it had no other role than to co-ordinate the work of civilian authorities in local communities, in municipalities, perhaps to interpret some decisions of the government and the Presidency, to point out shortcomings on the ground, and suggest solutions. And in addition to the commissions, therefore, there existed civilian authorities that did their job. The War Commission did not have the powers to replace them, except in those cases when those organs did not exist, were unable to meet or to operate; and in those cases, the War Commission had the power to take decisions that were in their competence. Such cases happened, but as far as I know not in Vogosca. In Vogosca, throughout the war, there was a municipal government that did its job. I believe this would be the short answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you explain where you physically sat, where you worked, in which period?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: In June I would go to Vogosca in the morning and return to Pale in the evening. After Vidovdan I stayed in the Park Hotel in Vogosca and I usually worked in an office in the Municipal Assembly, next to the office of the president of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever visit an institution in the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac, in particular any detention facility?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Never, not one. In Rajlovac, I went only to the central warehouse of the Red Cross to pick up some packages that I left to some starving people on my way back from Rajlovac to Pale. A friend of mine worked there, and I also met with a commissioner in Rajlovac, but not even in an office. We met as friends outside. I didn't visit any other institutions and I was not in contact with any military or other bodies in Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is satisfactory, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I noted that Mr. Karadzic addressed you as "President." Is it related to your position in law faculty now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the title of the president of the republic is for -- means for life that you can be addressed as "President."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I owe you an explanation. Since it goes beyond the period of the indictment, I did not insist on it, but Mr. Nikola Poplasen was the elected president of Republika Srpska in 1998, I believe, and on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Yes, Mr. Poplasen, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing, i.e., via your written statement instead of -- in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor Poplasen.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to start out by asking you just a few simple questions that perhaps you can confirm very briefly. You've never been a member of the SDS party; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, I was never a member.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in 1994 you were proclaimed a Chetnik Vojvoda; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And after a period of time in office as president of the Republika Srpska, you were removed from that office by the High Representative; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just to turn to your written statement, in paragraph 21 - and Dr. Karadzic alluded to it in the summary of your evidence - you described Karadzic as not being an authoritative leader and someone who couldn't entrench his authority at the required level. But, Professor, seven years ago when you came to testify in defence of Mr. Krajisnik, I noted that during your evidence in chief you described Dr. Karadzic's influence as "important" and "decisive." And that's at transcript page 20994, lines 11 and 12 of your evidence in the Krajisnik case. That's how you described him seven years ago; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: I suppose so, but I would have to refresh my memory, if that's how you read my evidence in the Krajisnik case. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It is. And I could show you the transcript page, Professor, but it's in English. I don't know if you're able to read English and I could read you the passage where you said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we upload it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That would be fine. That's 65 ter number --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't have to. You don't have to. I take your word for it. You don't have to read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And also in 2006, you answered a question from one of the Judges in the proceedings against Mr. Krajisnik and it was from His Honour Judge Hanoteau, and the question related to the relationship between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik. And you said, in contrast to what you said in your statement, that Mr. Karadzic was not only president of the republic, but also president of the SDS, the ruling party, which had absolute power. So that's what you said at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: All that is true, but I haven't yet heard a question. I suppose a question will follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in addition to this, rather than being a patient man, as you said of Dr. Karadzic in your statement at paragraph 21, in 2006 you said the following: "Mr. Karadzic hailed from the Dinara area which has this typical mind-set which is quite violent. So this is not just typical of him, it's rather typical of the area, and there's general agreement about this." So that's what you said at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: No. I certainly didn't use the term "nasilan," but "violentan" I suppose it's translated the same way.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have a look at the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could call it up, please. As I had indicated previously, 65 ter number 25650. And this is at transcript page 20993, and that might help any translation issues if we see the context within which the remark was made. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now if we can go down to line 14, I'll read you what that passage says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's read the question first.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The question you were given from Mr. Krajisnik's Defence counsel was: "Before we move away, so to speak, from Pale, you have described how you were in what I will call, using a colloquial English expression, the corridors of power for the short time in 1992. I would like you, please, to make an assessment of some of the people you rubbed shoulders with there and their influence, as far as you were concerned, with events and how they controlled events. "Firstly, Radovan Karadzic ..." And your answer was: "Generally speaking, numerous social and psychological studies of the populations of the Balkans indicate something that should be noted here. Mr. Karadzic hailed from the Dinara area which has this typical mind-set which is quite violent. So this is not just typical of him, it is rather typical of the area, and there is general agreement about this. I mention this because I wish to say that Mr. Karadzic was a typical representative of this mind-set characterised by large ideas and ambitions, more interested in visions than in practical problems." That was your characterisation of Dr. Karadzic in 2006?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: May I say something about this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, the whole thing revolves around the fact that I remember every word I said seven years later, and you see in this line it says "violent," whereas the interpreters here still say "nasilan." And "violentan," according to our Jovan Cvijic, our author, corresponds to a term which has nothing to do with violence. This is about a type of temperament that can express itself as I explained before, when Mr. Karadzic was prone to thunder when something was done wrong. It was not about violence as a feature, as a character trait, as a violent personality. And if I can add, I see the comment of the Prosecutor in the same light. Where she finds contradictions, I don't see any whatsoever. This was about my harmonious view. I was being asked here how I saw things, and I answered that Mr. Karadzic was too soft and too liberal. It is understood that it's from the point of view of my radical tastes. I'll try to be as brief as I can and finish. For example, I would never chair the meetings of the Main Board as he had. Those were endless discussions. All the members - and there were about a hundred - sometimes took the floor two or three times. No offence to any of the members, but even those who did not have any opinion took the floor and had something to say; and President Karadzic allowed it. He should have had more authority in a war-time situation on -- in my opinion. Authority is not used in the same sense in the Serbian language, in the sense of power. It is more used in the sense of good reputation, renown, somebody who commands authority and respect. In a war-time situation, decisions should have been taken more firmly, more quickly, without entering into any co-operation with the enemies of the Serbian people, without restoring your trust into somebody who had already tricked you many times before. That is the context. That is a comment that describes my characterisation of him as too democratic. I believe that a number of people would not find it too democratic, but it's not these people who are answering your questions now, it's me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But what I still don't understand, Professor, is that in 2006, seven years closer to the events we're talking about, you still described Dr. Karadzic's influence as being important and decisive and described the SDS as being the party in absolute power, in complete contrast to the characterisation you made in paragraph 21 of your statement. You spoke of Dr. Karadzic as a man in authority.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: May I? After all is said is done, all I believe is that you don't understand. Everything else is clear. Absolute power means that they had the absolute majority. I believe that needs no further proof. The SDS had all the important posts under its control. It had influence. I just explained to you. If he convinces the entire Main Board after that exhausting discussions, then the positions expressed by Dr. Karadzic are implemented. There are no other parties. There are no other influences. All the members of the Main Board, including the majority of the Assembly and all the officials, after all the arguments and exhausting debates, he succeeded in convincing them all of his ideas, in getting them to accept them. So I don't see why my statement that he was authoritative is in dispute. He had influence. The SDS had won the elections in a perfectly democratic way by winning the overwhelming majority, and it was therefore democratic. Why I minded these things I already said, and I told you what my objections to his style were. It was a constant weakness of the Serbian Democratic Party, this endless procrastination in the democratic process, although they believed that everything has to be perfectly clear, that all the arguments have to be put on the table, and that before implementation begins everyone has to agree. My own party worked a bit differently, and from that point of view I emphasised that my own practice was to allow people to take the floor if they really have something to say, not just to speak for the sake of speaking, of having fun. As for repetitions of things that have been said already, repeating common places from John Locke to our day, that can be left for later, talks over coffee. That was my point. But I didn't mean in my objection that he was a violent man. This was an interpretation of a term I used, and I can see that it's even written in English here "violent."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: "Violent" is something that denotes violence in the streets, something that is obvious, not something of theoretic relevance. My objection was not meant like that; it was meant entirely differently.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. I want to ask you -- actually, after this clarification, I want to put to you a remark that Jovan Tintor, who was the SDS president and the head of the Crisis Staff, you know, for the Serbian municipality of Vogosca, a remark that he made at a session of the Assembly of the Serbian People in April 1995. And he was talking about the period before the war. He said, and I'll quote: "I was ordered to create military formations. Perhaps you do not know it, General," because he was addressing General Mladic, "but I want you to know this: I went from municipality to municipality and created military formations on order from my president, and this is true. Here are people who know this to be the truth and have papers to prove it. We created brigade commanders down to platoon commanders, all this was done by the SDS."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that's at P970, English page 298 and B/C/S page 261.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you knew Mr. Tintor at the time. Professor, this is an example, what I've just read you, of Dr. Karadzic making his authority felt at the local level, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: I don't know what this has to do with my evidence. A statement made by some Tintor somewhere about something, and I hear it for the first time, by the way --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: I'm not saying that he had not said that. It's just that I hear it for the first time and I can't comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, you specifically said in paragraph 21 that Dr. Karadzic was unable to entrench his authority at the required level, and I've just read to you the words of a Vogosca municipal official who said that at the time it counted, Dr. Karadzic effectively made that authority felt. He went from municipality to municipality and created military formations on order from his president, that's Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: I can comment if you accept that I'm hearing this for the first time. I can comment but it doesn't mean that I witnessed it --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: -- I suppose that Jovan --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- Professor, my question was: These words are an example of Dr. Karadzic making his authority felt at the local level, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: No. If I may tell you why, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- please proceed, Mr. Poplasen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This statement by Jovan Tintor, I didn't see him around at that time or during the war either. When I came to Vogosca, he had left. I knew him before the war. Jovan Tintor was a house painter, the one who paints houses. He felt a need to build some sort of authority for himself rather than for Dr. Karadzic. I'm telling you what my comment about this is. He probably used the opportunity of attention or confrontation with General Mladic in order to prove himself more important than his officers. He didn't have any opportunity to command brigades or battalions; that can only happen in cartoons. And it sounds like a construction which should now be taken as a fact in order to explain what was going on. I know what was going on on the ground. Mladic and his generals were so authoritative -- authoritarian, actually, in the military sense, in the sense of army subordination. Any opposition was eliminated. Tintor was no officer; he's a house painter. The civilian authorities did not have any military competence and Tintor's statement could only serve for him to show off, like a peacock when it spreads its tail, at this meeting, so that somebody would like him, so that he would expand his ego and perhaps build his authority among the civilian authorities. I can't view that in any different way.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we have a break?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have -- yes, a follow-up question. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, but given the length of time the answer might take, perhaps it's better to pause now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.05.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before we move on, Professor, I just wanted to stay with the statement by Mr. Tintor we were talking about before the break, where you said he didn't have the opportunity to command brigades and battalions because that only happens in cartoons and that the civilians had no military competence. Professor, shortly after Mr. Tintor made that statement in the Bosnian Serb Assembly session, the 50th Session in April 1995, Dr. Karadzic actually responded. And I'll tell you -- I'll quote to you what Dr. Karadzic said. On pages 323 and 324 of the English translation of P970, Dr. Karadzic said: "It was the SDS which organised the people and created the army. It was an army. Together with the police, those who were the armed forces of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, they created the space, liberated, and created the space." And he goes on to say: "We decided to set up the TO, the Serbian brigades, which were indeed led by the SDS but not as a party army, but as a people's army, for not everyone dared to put himself at the head of an illegal brigade and oppose the Green Berets, like Jovan Tintor, who impoverished himself in this war and we're quick to label Jovan Tintor who gave everything for this party, for this people. We're quick to call him a profiteer or something like that." So, Professor, Dr. Karadzic himself confirmed what Mr. Tintor said, so it seems that you're not only wrong in your assertion that the civilian authorities had no military competence, you were also -- your assertion that Mr. Tintor had no military command was speculation; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would you like to explain?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Of course. If I had been in the situation which Dr. Karadzic was, when did you say, 1995, I would have had the same thing, only I would have put a little bit more of edge into it because he referred to the laws that were then in force. In the indictment you have a combination of provisions about Territorial Defence with a newly formed army. The obligation of the civilian authorities in every crisis situation is to mobilise the so-called Territorial Defence. It was a part of the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Yugoslavia; there's nothing problematic about that --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Professor --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: You placed the emphasis on the first several sentences, claiming that the last sentence in Dr. Karadzic's speech is marginal, whereas it's crucial. This has to do with the Territorial Defence, which was set up in accordance with regulations in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the regulations of the Republic of Yugoslavia, which was then still in existence. This Territorial Defence has certain obligations and tasks which were defined by the law, inter alia, it is organised for various purposes --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Professor, are you saying that when Dr. Karadzic confirmed that the Serbian brigades were led by the SDS and that Jovan Tintor put himself at the head of a brigade to oppose the Green Berets, are you saying that when Dr. Karadzic confirmed that he was lying?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: No. The Serbian Democratic Party was part of the authorities; that's what he had in mind, part of the state authorities, not as the Serbian Democratic Party. He's here so let him explain what he was doing at the time. I'm not his Defence counsel. As a part of the authorities, it was their duty to organise the Territorial Defence, not as the Serbian Democratic Party. And as for the fact that he shortened the discussion in his speeches, you don't think that he could read all the provisions of the law to the deputies and teach them the ABC of law --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: -- as someone who was participating in power -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I can't find your passage in the -- pages referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, that I've given the wrong page numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please check. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I will absolutely do that. I miss my colleague beside me, but I will get back to you with that as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Professor, if I could move on because I think -- with respect, Professor, I think we're getting far and away outside of the question that I've asked you. And I'd like to go into another area of your statement and that's at paragraphs 5 and 6, where you were asked about the role, if any, of the municipal Crisis Staffs and War Presidencies in Serb-sought and Serb-controlled areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the persecution of non-Serbs. And also related to the area I'm going to deal with now is paragraph 15, where you said that any restrictions imposed were implemented equally to everyone. And before I ask you some -- show you some documents in that regard, I'd like to go back to your Krajisnik testimony in front of this Tribunal in 2006.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'll actually ask for the page to be pulled up, that's 65 ter number 25650, page 21097.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There, during your testimony as a Defence witness in the Krajisnik trial, His Honour Judge Orie asked you: "Did ethnic cleansing," and that's at line 6. "Did ethnic cleansing occur in the territory in -- under the control of the Bosnian Serb forces in 1992?" And your answer was "no." So your position in 2006 in front of this Tribunal was that no ethnic cleansing occurred in territory controlled by Bosnian Serb forces in 1992; right? We see it on the page there in front of us.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Well, you see, but my answer is not as you said. It says here "in my opinion." Not just "no" and nothing but.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine. That's correct, that reflected your position in 2006; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move on to some documents now. I'd like to show you, Professor, P2638. It's a decision dated 23 July 1992 by the Celinac War Presidency and it's distributed to the local SJB and the military command, which we see later in the document, as well as all households. And this decision, Professor, gives the non-Serb population on the territory of the municipality special status. If we could have a look at Article 5 on page 2 of this document in both languages, I think, we see in Article 5 that non-Serbs are under a curfew between 4.00 and 6.00 p.m. [sic]. They can't linger in public places. They can't bathe in the rivers, hunt, they can't fish. They can't gather in groups of more than three men. They can't sell real estate or exchange flats without permission from the competent organ. But, you see, Article 4, immediately above that, says they can leave so long as they all go, the entire household goes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Did it apply to all non-Serb population, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could go over to the Article 1, Your Honour, because you see clause 5 refers to the citizens from Article 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The decision refers specifically to the status of the non-Serbian population of Celinac municipality, and Article 1 specifically refers as well to non-Serb population of Celinac municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not limited to only the individuals referred to in Article 2?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we go back over to Article 5, we see that that's not the case. And an examination of the document in full, Your Honour, actually shows specific references to the particular citizens identified in Article 2 in any number of other clauses, apart from the references that we're dealing with here which refer to Article 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Professor, so first of all this decision - and it's not from the military, it's from the War Presidency - specifically applies to non-Serbs who are restricted in any number of ways that have nothing to do with military operations. So, Professor, your evidence that any restrictions were implemented equally to everyone is actually completely incorrect and this document shows that.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is a discriminatory decision and it discriminates against non-Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would you like to explain why you feel that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: You can see that it says in Article 4 that the competent organs shall provide the necessary documentation and ensure safe passage. The necessary documentation probably implies the state-issued documents issued by the municipalities. I suppose, because I wasn't in Celinac at the time, the safe passage probably implies the route which would not be threatened by anyone and which would enable them to pass along a route of their choice. And as for Article 5, I don't know, perhaps it all has to do with some situations in Celinac where the idea was to protect these people. Maybe there were groups which were attacking non-Serbian populations so it was necessary to save the people's lives. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Professor --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: -- I'm just speculating. You presented this document to me and offered just one possible interpretation; however, there are many more possible interpretations.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Professor, I'm not going to ask you to speculate; I didn't ask you to speculate and I don't want a speculative answer, with respect. So what we're going to do is we're going to move on to another document. I'd like to take us, actually, to 65 ter number 05119. It's a document dated 14 July 1992, and it's an extract from the minutes of the War Staff for Sanski Most municipality. Item 1 of this document records the decision of the War Staff that public sector employees of Serbian nationality whose war time assignment takes them away from their work-place are on paid leave, while Croats and Muslims are on unpaid leave. So, Professor, this is not a decision affecting everyone equally, is it? Croats and Muslims are treated differently, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Judging by this document, it is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's a discriminatory decision, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Judging by this document -- I'm speculating. You keep asking me -- first you presented to me Celinac, then Sanski Most, where I've never been in my life, and you insist that I should speculate. I don't know what other answer is possible. Neither was I there, nor do I know these people, nor am I familiar with this. How could I testify about this on the basis of my experience? You can write whatever you like and ask me whether this deserves to be condemned. If it was like this on the ground, then it does deserve to be condemned, but I don't know what this has to do -- at least I don't understand what this has to do with my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, your testimony, your testimony -- in paragraph 15 of your statement you were specifically asked whether Serb authorities in the RS imposed or maintained discriminatory measures against the non-Serb population. And your response was that -- was no, was that any restrictions that were implemented applied equally to everyone. This document shows your assertion is incorrect, you're wrong?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: No, you're coming back to it again. You asked me, judging by my experience and in my view -- well, you want to refute my experience by a document which is completely independent from this experience and which was created several hundred kilometres away. So other witnesses will have to confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You gave evidence in the Krajisnik case, Professor, that through 1992, you travelled across the breadth of Bosnian Serb-held territory establishing the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just -- I have to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we upload his statement, and in the meantime I would like his statement, hard copy, to be provided to him. Paragraph 15. Do you see your statement, paragraph 15?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could have a quick look.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is in general to the effect that there was no discrimination, in particular the last sentence reads like this: "The only decisions that do perhaps exist are those relating to curfews, issued by the military organs, but these were valid for everyone." But the document you saw in relation to Celinac was a bit different. If that was true, then your statement is not correct; do you agree with it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This statement of mine has to do with my experience in Vogosca, and I can't assess and evaluate events which took place far away from where I was and far away from my experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the question was formulated as regards the whole municipalities or Republika Srpska as a whole.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. This primarily has to do with Vogosca and my experience there. These generalisations follow from my experience in Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Professor, now that you've limited your evidence in regard to -- in paragraph 15 in regard to the situation in Vogosca, perhaps we could go over to paragraphs 5 and 6 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you have your statement with you now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The question you were asked in paragraph 5 was whether Crisis Staffs existed and operated at any point in the Serbian municipalities, and, as far as you know, whether they served as the means for the permanent removal of non-Serbs from areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina which the Bosnian Serbs claimed as theirs through various means. Is your answer also in relation to question 5 limited to the situation in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is generalised, as I said a little while ago, on the basis of my experience in Vogosca, to the extent that the listener wants to hear that it's generalised, but it originates from this particular experience. And in several places you can see "according to my knowledge," "according to my experience," that can be found in my answer. "As far as I know."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, in paragraph 6 of your statement, you were similarly asked whether you had any information on the reasons for establishing War Presidencies in the municipalities and how they functioned. And you didn't qualify your answer in that paragraph in any regard whatsoever.
