You said: "As with the Crisis Staffs, the War Presidencies were a form of organising government in the emerging situation and they had no specific role, particularly not in regard to planning the persecution of the non-Serb population." Are you now here limiting your answer to this question to the situation in Vogosca municipality during the period of time in which you served as war commissioner?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is my experience. Of course, it is my rational supposition that the Crisis Staff and then the War Presidency -- or, rather, the war commissioner's office in Vogosca was the outcome of a document which served as the basis for establishing Crisis Staffs and war commissions in other municipalities as well. In accordance with the principle of analogy, the events should have been similar in other municipalities, but I cannot confirm that on the basis of my own experience but only on the basis of the assumption that others honoured the documents issued by the Presidency and the government and that they worked accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for just a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when you in your statement in paragraph 5 said: "Population relocation took place on all sides throughout the war, but this was merely and solely a result of the security problems arising from the chaos," do you similarly now limit that generalisation to refer solely to the situation in Vogosca municipality?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: No. I know for certain that this was taking place in most of the territory of the republic, that people chose a place of residence where, justifiably or not, they felt more secure, more safe, where they had different prospects where they could find jobs and various other things. I was one of them. I suppose I know why I left Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, since this generalisation is -- well, since you've not limited this to Vogosca municipality, perhaps I could ask you a question about that. Your written evidence actually says you went up to Banja Luka in 1993, and maybe we can talk for a minute about what was going on while you were there in the city. Professor, this Chamber has received evidence that throughout 1994, Bosnian Serb authorities were taking part in a campaign of continuing human rights abuses of minorities in Banja Luka from February right through to September.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that's -- that evidence is found in Exhibits D3492 at page 4, paragraph 14; P5423; and P2087.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Professor, in September, over 2.500 Muslim civilians, we've heard, were forcefully expelled from Bijeljina and Janja and almost 1.000 similar departures took place from Banja Luka to Croatia. So the evidence is that this was a practice that had been underway for at least eight months and it was at a level that attracted international attention, and despite repeated protests -- the policy and the expulsions actually accelerated. So, Professor, over two years into the war, when the RS institutions were functioning, these forced transfers aren't a reflection of chaos, are they?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that with the example of Sarajevo. There, in this way, as you describe, more than 100.000 people left the city. That's closer to my experience. As for Banja Luka, I was in opposition at the time and I worked at the university so I didn't follow what was going on. But I did experience this, so it's a bit of a problem where you choose to focus your attention. We can investigate why more than 100.000 Serbs were forced to leave Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My -- my question --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Or perhaps they --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question was specifically related to the expulsion of over 1.000 people in Banja Luka in September 1994, Professor. My question -- because you were there at that time. My question has nothing to do with Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Well, I was sitting in my office in Banja Luka at the faculty of law, but I had images of Sarajevo. That was my experience too.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: My answer is a direct answer to your question, not in terms of your expectations, no, but it is responsive to your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And now, having touched on that, I'm going to move on to something you discussed at paragraphs 10 and 11 of your statement. And there you talked about detention facilities in Vogosca, and you discuss those in the Krajisnik case as well, during your testimony there, and that was in the Krajisnik case in specific reference to the facility you visited, Sonja's. So, Professor, in the Krajisnik case you confirmed that the people you saw being detained there were civilians; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in your evidence in the Krajisnik case, you agreed that the detention of civilians was a crime; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: I don't know how you use this notion of captivity. I just said that I remember my testimony. I said that they had not been locked up. I haven't got that paper here with me, my testimony in Krajisnik, but I remember that I described the situation as people walking about freely in front of the building and that my impression was that they were waiting for transportation or something like that. There was no key, that people stopped to have breakfast or tea or something like that, whereas you keep referring to captivity. This was a facility where people came from different directions, and then they were probably -- well, that was not my affair. I just stopped by to have breakfast and then I went on. It wasn't my job to record that, to process that or to make any decisions; however, what I saw is along those lines. I don't think that "imprisonment" or "captivity" would be the right word; that means that somebody had been had been arrested and locked up, and that was not the case there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have a look again at the transcript of the Professor's evidence in the Krajisnik case, please; 65 ter 25650 at page 21138.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Professor, at lines 11 to 15 of this document, His Honour Judge Hanoteau asked you whether -- and in specific reference to Sonja's whether: "For you, was the fact of being deprived freedom of your citizens, if it wasn't legal, was this for you a particularly important crime?" And your answer was: "Yes, it is a crime." Those were your words; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: I don't see my entire statement here. You see, in part it had to do with the suggestion that there were other places of detention in Vogosca, not the Sonja facility that you're referring to. I assume that this refers to these other places, this question, and then I stand by that answer that I gave. My reaction was that I did not visit these facilities and I did not know where they were. My reaction was to the fact that I may have heard that this existed, I informed the Ministry of Justice, and I asked for that to be integrated into the legal system, because if that were not done, then that would be a crime indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you reported that, as you've indicated in your statement, not only to the Ministry of Justice, you reported that to the Presidency, didn't you? You reported the detention of civilians at the location you saw to the Presidency; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: No, I did not report detention. I said that this existed. As far as I knew, the facility that was supposed to be a prison, although it was not part of legal system, the Presidency should find a solution so that the Ministry of Justice could integrate it into the legal system. I never said that I went to that facility that constituted a prison, because I was duty-bound to trust my co-workers. If they told me that that exists, then it existed, and then I reacted in this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we see P2371, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Professor, do you recognise your letter to the war-time Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina about the prison in Vogosca? Paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise that. This just confirms what I said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You reported the existence of this facility to the Presidency, that's what this letter says, and you recommended the Ministry of Justice be assigned with the task of integrating it; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Professor, this Chamber has received evidence that after the date of this letter, civilians who were detained at Sonja's were transferred to another facility in the village of Svrake, Planjo's house, and they were detained there for months. And during those months, they were repeatedly taken by Serb forces for work and that work included doing labour on the front line and being used as human shields on the front line. And as a result of that work in dangerous situations, people were killed and wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that evidence, Your Honours, is found in P44, P2361, P42, and those are statements, Your Honours; and documents recording the use of prisoners in various situations are - and I won't name all of them - P45, P1144, P2387 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please concentrate on asking the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Professor, the use of civilians at dangerous front line positions where they would be killed or wounded is a crime, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: It's that way all over the world, isn't it, including Libya, Iraq, Afghanistan, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you agree, your answer is yes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, I just want to have a look at one of the documents that was associated to your witness statement that you commented on, which is 1D09197, please. Now, Professor, you never saw this document until you were shown it in preparation for your testimony here today; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Professor, this Chamber's received evidence that these 150 people that the document refers to who were captured were captured in the attack on Svrake on 2nd of May. They were being held in Naka's garage, which was near the Vogosca overpass, and after this order was issued, the prisoners weren't released, they were moved to Planjo's house. Professor, you commented on the document not knowing a single thing about the matters discussed on the paper in front of you; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: It is correct -- well, I don't know. How come I don't know? Of course, I didn't sign this but a member of the commission, I guess I was absent. What is being insisted upon here is lawful procedure. Now your question is focused on unlawful transfer from Podvoznja [phoen] to some prison. I really don't know anything about that. I didn't see that, I don't have any knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you can confirm that you commented on the document, not knowing a single thing about it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: I commented upon the document, not the actual events. The document was signed by a member of the commission and I was his superior, and I was probably absent from Vogosca. I was probably away.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Professor, the document's a cover-up. These people were never released, and you said in your statement that they were. You said, and I'll quote you, paragraph 25: "It can be seen from the document that about 10 per cent of the people were kept for further investigation, whereas the others were brought back to their homes accompanied by security." The evidence is, Professor, that's not true. This document's a cover-up, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: No, this document is supposed to be a contribution to the creation of a state based on rule of law. Now, the fact that you are linking this to something that has nothing to do with it is something that I really have to react to. How can this be a cover-up when the signatories of the document do not have any knowledge about certain events that you are linking this to? Things that happened even after the document was created. So you're even linking this up subsequently. The document was written up. People were supposed to behave in a lawful way, and then months later something happens and then you subsequently link this to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have your statement, Mr. Poplasen, paragraph 25?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you read the last sentence. Could you read it aloud, the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 25 you said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was shown document 1D9197, from which it can be seen that before my arrival the municipal authorities had already began regulating legal status of the detainees and POWs. It can be seen from the document that about 10 per cent of the people were kept for further criminal investigation, whereas the others were brought back to their homes accompanied by security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we should take a look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue. Yes, my question was whether the information in the last sentence, i.e., 10 per cent being kept for further criminal investigation while remaining were brought back being accompanied by security, where did you get this information from this document? How could it be seen from this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's written there. It can be seen from the document. I'd have to look at the document. I'd have to look at these numbers. Probably in this improvised agreement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please read the document and let us know. We can collapse it in English and blow up the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. The prison warden is ordered to release from the prison in Svrake 541 persons. The warden is duty-bound to safely transport them to their destination. 20 persons remain. As for their status, the warden will take care. The warden is duty-bound to take some written statements in view of their status that they had during their stay in prison. The persons are -- well, what is written here is -- well, it says 20 persons remain in prison; isn't that right? Or if it hasn't been typed up properly, there's a smudge here, maybe the number is bigger, I concluded obviously that that was about 10 per cent of 1.451. It's not that I calculated it specifically, that's why it says "approximately," not "exactly."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask for this to be spelled out precisely. Let's have a look at the translation. How is that written, 154?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It must be 154 because this is the letter L over here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I'll leave it at that. Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, just one small area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could have a look, please, at another one of your associated documents. It's 65 ter number 1566. It's an extract of an interview with Rajko Koprivica, who was the head of the Executive Board in Vogosca, dated 13 June 1992. Your statement actually says July, but I think we'll find that it's June.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if we could go over to page 6 of the English translation of this document and page 2 of the B/C/S version, and on page 2 we should magnify the bottom right area, if I have this correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Poplasen, in paragraph 7 of your statement, you said that between the first armed clashes and the middle of 1993, Vogosca had no electricity. And in this interview, Mr. Koprivica in June of 1992 was asked whether he read the daily newspaper "Nas glas" or he listened to Serbian radio and watched Serbian TV. And he said: "Whenever possible I also listened to the radio," and that he rarely watches TV - if we can go up to the top of the right-hand column on the English page - because Serbian television in -- he rarely watches Serbian TV as the reception in Vogosca is rather poor. So this is a document that you -- actually you embraced and you commented on extensively in your statement. Now, having looked at that, I want to go to one more about electricity and it's 65 ter number 25633. It's an excerpt -- another excerpt from "Nas glas" daily newspaper in Vogosca, and it's dated 9 November 1992. And the square on the bottom right-hand side of the page in your language contains a notice from the electrical distribution company asking Serbian -- citizens of the Serbian municipality of Vogosca to limit their consumption of electricity as much as possible or they're going to be forced to introduce power cuts reducing consumption in certain areas. So two documents we've just seen, one of them being a document you specifically commented on, actually contradict your statement as regards the lack of electricity in Vogosca completely, Mr. Poplasen.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Well, these are not exactly documents of major importance. I was there all the time and I know with certainty that there was no electricity and no hot water. As for this statement made by Mr. Koprivica, there were generators and they could generate electricity someplace for a certain amount of time, especially if there was fuel. Then also there were batteries and there were some kind of supply systems apart from the distribution network. As for November and this information that you referred to, perhaps that was a result of my intervention to the Presidency. You see, the Presidency wasn't supposed to report to me; I was supposed to report to them. I wanted them to deal with the problems of Hadzici, Rajlovac, Vogosca, Ilidza, the distribution of electricity, supplies, organising economic life and so on. I assume that this was one of the first attempts made by Elektrodistribucija for the network to start functioning. And already in November perhaps there was power for about an hour or two. Citizens were able to have electricity at least a little bit and still there were reductions. Also, all the time when I went to Vogosca, I know for sure that there wasn't electricity anywhere. There wasn't any hot water anywhere. And during the night we had to make do, but there was no electricity from the system. As for these documents that deviate from my own experience, well, good luck to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have this last excerpt admitted as a Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6511, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if I could just have a moment to find something in the transcript of previous testimony, Your Honours, I'll be very brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just to clear up the record, in fact, Mr. Poplasen, you indicated that -- during your testimony in the Krajisnik case, you indicated that you only visited Vogosca from time to time because of your work, among other things, travelling around the country to institute or to establish the Serbian Radical Party; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, in the Krajisnik case you said one "could say that I was there quite rarely, not really often." And that's at transcript page 20959, line 15. Those were your words; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't have any other questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any further examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Very few, Excellency, very few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, when you said that with regard to the competences of the Crisis Staff and the exercise of authority that you inferred on the basis of analogy, tell us this: In some municipality if things were not done as they were done in Vogosca, as prescribed by the central organs, did this aberration come from the system or from where?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: The way I see things and on the basis of my experience, if you are referring to infractions and violations of the law, they were primarily due to lack of knowledge, stubbornness, and also some criminal aspirations every now and then by individuals at local level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the document, or rather, in your testimony, 25650, on page 21138, Judge Hanoteau put a question to you, whether depriving civilians of their liberty was a crime unless that was lawful and your answer was "yes." Were you informed at the time that somebody had been detained on an illegal basis?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: I did not know of illegal detention. As far as Vogosca is concerned, if that's what you mean, when I was informed that there was some detention, in a split second or even during the course of a single day, I cannot establish whether it's lawful or unlawful, that has to be done by the investigation organs, whether there are legal grounds for detention; however, it's not local activists or the local police service or the local army that can determine that. That has to be determined through appropriate judicial proceedings, and that is why I insisted that this be integrated into the legal system, into the justice system. So it's very hard for me now, I mean some specific name, when I am not aware of these specific names in these specific cases. Had I known, I would have reacted individually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This answer of yours then, was it a principled answer to a principled question or was it a response to this specific situation?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: It was an answer in principle, in general. It covers all the rest and I hoped when saying it that the same was being done in all the local communities in other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In pages 53 and 54, esteemed Mrs. Edgerton asked you a very complex question and then concluded with a generalised question: Would taking civilians to do work on front lines constitute a crime? At the time were you informed that somebody was taking civilians to front lines?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: If I may put it this way, it's a malicious formulation, taking civilians to the front line. Speaking of what I know, it was about a law on mobilise -- of mobilisation of military conscripts. There was a legal framework and they went to work, if they did, and returned home and received appropriate remuneration and were given appropriate safety. Now, the fact that those people who went to work did not have rifles or uniforms is used in this question to interpret that they were civilians. They were Muslims and -- but they still had a military obligation. As far as I know, those who were engaged as part of the work obligation still had that military obligation and they were given proper security, they were given proper remuneration, and they returned home after work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that Serbs had a military obligation which was harder than the work obligation?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know what my position was concerning ethnic cleansing? Did I favour the expulsion of Croats and Muslims from Serbian territory?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You don't know my position or ...?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: What I know is that I did not hear myself that you insisted on any ethnic-based persecution or expulsion. On the contrary you insisted that a large number of members of other ethnic communities, including Muslims and Croats, who were in the Territorial Defence, in the VRS, enjoy the same treatment and that they must not be in a less privileged position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In what position were the citizens who did not have to fulfil their military obligation but still had a work obligation, were they discriminated against?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: I think it was actually positive discrimination. Army service was much more dangerous. People got killed, people got wounded, which is not the case with the work obligation. In the work obligation we even tried to secure proper nutrition, to supply food, which was not always possible with the front lines. So it was a privilege to be in the work obligation. I spent most of the war in work obligation duties, so I know the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you had managed to establish what my view was of violent, unlawful acts against Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand. Against Serbs who committed such violent acts or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In general, violent acts, criminal acts against Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: I know that you insisted on the legal procedure, that perpetrators be prosecuted, but I'm not sure that the justice system had the capability to respond quickly enough, to make decisions in an efficient, expedient way that would be satisfactory to everyone. I don't have the records with me, but I know that we had many prosecutions against Serb criminals and thugs even during the war to prosecute them for acts against members of other ethnic communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of your role and the fact that you were sent to the local level by the representatives of the republic, what did you expect from the local authorities vis-à-vis perpetrators of crimes against Croats and Muslims? Did you expect --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm not sure if this was originating or arising from the cross-examination. Was that your point?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Exactly my point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think this does arise from the implication about Dr. Karadzic having this violent proclivity. I think that this goes to the idea of whether Dr. Karadzic in his instructions and his assignment of this individual to do a job in Vogosca, whether he was in favour of or against violent crimes against non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll allow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat, Mr. President. In view of the role that the Presidency asked you to discharge on the ground, can you tell us what did central authorities expect from local authorities regarding crimes against Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: The central authorities - and of course I spoke directly to you and Mr. Koljevic, who was in charge - had a rather idealistic view and they wanted full affirmation of the rule of law, but that was not feasible at the time. It arose probably from an ambition to regulate things in such a way that laws can operate without hindrance. And this interview we had seen with Mr. Koprivica, as far as I remember, is to a great extent the result of my lecturing and explanations to the leadership of the municipalities. I tried to explain to them what the legal system for local authorities should be, what equal treatment of everyone means, and these ideas can be found here. That's the same way I intervened with the local authorities and the same way I wrote my reports to the government regarding what arrangements and solutions should be put in place for the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My last question: You mentioned Jovan Cvijic. Could you tell the Chamber briefly who was Jovan Cvijic and what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Where did that happen? Where was Jovan Cvijic mentioned during the course of today at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you were asked, Mr. President, about the short-tempered mentality of people from the Dinara mountains, you mentioned Jovan Cvijic and it was --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you, it's on page 30 or 31.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me just finish the question. The interpreters, trying to find a better term in Serbian, used the word "silovit" instead of "nasilan." Could you find a synonym for the word you actually used?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: I reacted because of this bad interpretation, and it's not the first time. The interpreters and the Prosecutor could have found a different term. I didn't say "oppressive" or "repressive," but I said "violentan." That is a part of the characterology of the Balkan peoples described by a great scientist and the first president of the Serb academy of arts and sciences, Jovan Cvijic in his famous tome that is still used in schools that study this subject. When one says "violentan" it means not unjust, not unfair, it doesn't mean destructive, it means short-fused. A person who reacts quickly but fairly. And after this quick, initial reaction, that person usually calms down and apologises. And these reactions are usually to the violation of legal and -- norms and norms of fairness, requiring a proper procedure that would lead to proper sanctions and punishment. It doesn't mean a violent reaction. It is the opposite of "sang froid," unemotional people who are able to observe an unfair, an unjust situation for a long time and take a longer time to react.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, for your efforts, despite your health problems. Thank you for coming here to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Poplasen. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. You are free to go. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- Your Honours, with regard to the incorrect citation I gave you for P970, my apologies, I was working off a version -- a translation that was not filed in evidence. The filed -- or admitted into evidence. The admitted translation has that citation at pages 316 and 317 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it we do not have further witnesses for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There's one matter I'd like to raise with you, Mr. Robinson. As you have seen, the Appeals Chamber has issued its decision on the Tolimir appeal. Before we going back to dealing with the Mladic and Stanisic subpoena motions, we wanted to check if you perhaps had another discussion with the counsel for Mr. Mladic and Mr. Stanisic, and whether in light of the Tolimir decision Mr. Mladic and Mr. Stanisic were now willing to come and give evidence voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have had those discussions, and at this stage neither of them are willing to testify voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Unless there are further matters to be discussed, raised, today, until Monday morning the hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 18th day of November, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.26 p.m.,
